taxonomic_note: Accepted species but non-native in Texas.
look_here_first: KLEINGRASS: INTRODUCED African perennial forage TUFT, often tall and knotty at its center, with fine open branching panicles. Look for firm basal perennial growth, then confirm Panicum spikelet anatomy and collar. Existing two real photos show general habit, NOT precise ligule, glume length or crown cross section; never treat the naturalized Texas presence as county-native evidence.

project_inclusion.range_basis: Kew/POWO accepts Panicum coloratum but gives its native range as Egypt to southern Africa and explicitly lists Texas as introduced. Texas A&M Rangelands describes Kleingrass as an introduced warm-season perennial brought from Africa. Texas specimen records, including Hays County, are introduced/naturalized occurrences and therefore do not count toward the project native threshold.
project_inclusion.range_guardrail: Occurrence is not treated as nativity; introduced records do not count toward the three-county native threshold.

morphology_keys.joey_family_training: Poaceae family training: identify inflorescence architecture first, then inspect spikelets/glumes/lemma-palea/awns and ligule-collar-sheath characters.

crew_field_check: KLEINGRASS: INTRODUCED African perennial forage TUFT, often tall and knotty at its center, with fine open branching panicles. Look for firm basal perennial growth, then confirm Panicum spikelet anatomy and collar. Existing two real photos show general habit, NOT precise ligule, glume length or crown cross section; never treat the naturalized Texas presence as county-native evidence.

Unlike short native blue-gray P. hallii, Kleingrass often makes substantial robust cultivated or naturalized bunches; unlike witchgrass it is perennial without coarse hairy annual stems; unlike rhizomatous switchgrass don't infer a switchgrass white collar patch from a small panoramic photo.
Examine the same plant's crown, collar and mature spikelet with a millimeter scale before assigning difficult specimens.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Panicum virgatum: Switchgrass is native, rhizomatous, and has a characteristic hairy collar; Kleingrass is introduced and typically has a firm knotty base. Panicum hallii: Hall's panicum is smaller, glaucous and native, with a more compact stiff-branched panicle.

field_id_lesson.look_here_first: Kleingrass is an introduced perennial forage bunchgrass with a firm often knotty crown and an open, fine-branched panicle. Confirm at collar and mature spikelet; do not confuse with native switchgrass.

measured_checks.growth: Perennial tuft, often knotty at base.
measured_checks.ligule: Hair-fringed ligule; macro and scale needed.
measured_checks.panicle: Open, diffuse; document full length and branch attachment.
measured_checks.spikelets: Small, generally a few millimeters; measure before final identification.
measured_checks.glumes: Lower glume notably shorter than spikelet in published keys; verify proportion on mature spikelet.
measured_checks.lemma: Inspect fertile upper floret and lower sterile lemma; close macro needed.
measured_checks.awns: No awn inference from distant panicle images.

measured_diagnostic_key_20261023.look_here_first: KLEINGRASS: trace an open 4–30 cm panicle to a rooted, knotty perennial TUFT, then measure solitary, awnless 2–3.2 mm spikelets. The LOWER glume is only about one-quarter to one-third of spikelet length; don't confuse this introduced forage grass with native Hall's panicgrass or switchgrass by head shape alone.
measured_diagnostic_key_20261023.growth_form: Introduced African tufted perennial, sometimes shortly rhizomatous; stems often 15–100 cm but taller in some regional treatments. Confirm attached perennial crown rather than inferring it from a cut flowering culm.
measured_diagnostic_key_20261023.ligule_collar: True ligule is a ciliate-edged membrane; regional treatments give approximately 0.5–2.5 mm (VicFlora), while Flora of China gives 0.5–1 mm. Blades generally 2–12 mm wide, with sheath hairiness variable. Photograph the true blade–sheath junction separately from any neighboring sheath hairs.
measured_diagnostic_key_20261023.panicle_spikelets: Open to partly contracted branched panicle usually 4–30 cm; spikelets solitary, pedicelled, ovate-elliptic, approximately 2–3.2 mm, dorsally compressed, awnless. Panicle silhouette alone is not species-diagnostic.
measured_diagnostic_key_20261023.glumes: Lower glume cufflike, approximately 0.7–1 mm, generally 1-veined (occasionally up to 3), only one-quarter to one-third of mature spikelet length. Upper glume approximately spikelet-length, 7–9-veined.
measured_diagnostic_key_20261023.lemmas_palea_awns: Lower floret is staminate in cited treatments, with membranous lower lemma approximately spikelet-length and a developed palea. Upper fertile lemma approximately 1.5–2.5 mm, firm, smooth, shiny and inrolled around palea. No true awns; do not label slender panicle pedicels as awns.
measured_diagnostic_key_20261023.central_texas_lookalikes: P. hallii is typically smaller, stiff, blue-glaucous and basal-leaved; P. capillare is a hairy annual with diffuse tumbleweed-like head; P. virgatum is usually rhizomatous with a characteristic triangular white-hair patch on upper blade base. Verify roots, ligule and spikelet glumes rather than using height or forage habitat alone.

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Kleingrass — verify forage bunch then obtain real panicle and ligule anatomy
steps: ARCHIVED EVIDENCE: panels 0–1 teach the overall forage habit; panel 6 is an ACTUAL lifted root crown with fibrous roots photographed by Harry Rose in Australia as var. makarikariense. This corrects the old 'no photographed roots' claim but does not provide a Texas rooted voucher. Panels 2 and 4 show true ligule-region hairs and exterior collar respectively, without a measured membrane tip.

VARIETY HOLD: Harry Rose identified the photographed plant as Panicum coloratum var. makarikariense, NOT a Texas-vouchered representative of any variety. Do not project subtle variety-level anatomy to an unvouchered Hays plant.

LOCAL COLLAR PHOTOS: physically archived Australian var. makarikariense panel 2 shows the inner ligule region and hairs; panel 4 shows the outer collar. The free membranous ligule length is not independently measurable without a real ruler, and these photographs do not identify a Texas variety.

LOCAL REPRODUCTIVE PHOTO: physically archived Australian var. makarikariense panel 5 shows genuine attached purple spikelets. Panel 3 is a separate external thumbnail from the same variety, not a dissection. Neither establishes individual glume/lemma dimensions or local Texas identity.
THIRD examine the separately identified Panicum hallii look-alike: its smaller rocky-site basal clump and curling dried leaf blades can be suggestive but size and dry leaf curl are not decisive.
FOURTH photograph a genuine mature P. coloratum panicle on the same documented plant from full-branch and 10–20× views; retain spikelets on the stalk and measure their length with a 1-mm ruler.

FIFTH split the fresh same-plant blade–sheath junction to show actual membranous/ciliate ligule, collar, sheath hairs and nodes; dissect and photograph measured glumes, sterile floret and shiny fertile lemma before asserting species.

LAST-MILE PHOTO GAPS: a locally authenticated Texas root-to-head flowering plant, its opened measured true inner ligule, ripe dissected glumes and lower/upper lemmas with mm ruler, and matched native P. hallii / P. virgatum comparisons. The Australian photographed rooted crown (panel 6) already supplies an educational example of actual root structure, but does not close the Texas voucher gap.

Confirm a Texas plant using a matched rooted flowering voucher with measured true inner ligule and mature spikelet anatomy; do not infer local variety or native status from Australian reference photographs.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST — KLEINGRASS BUNCH
field_id_short_tiles.short: Introduced perennial: trace the fine open panicle to a firm, knotty rooted tuft.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Kleingrass is an introduced African forage perennial, sometimes shortly rhizomatous, with an open 4–30 cm branching panicle. USDA and CC0 panels 0–1 teach the broad habit but do not expose roots. Harry Rose's panel 6 actually exposes a rooted knotty crown with attached fibrous roots from AUSTRALIAN var. makarikariense; this is real structural evidence, NOT a locally vouchered Texas root-to-head specimen. Never diagnose from pasture setting or one distant silhouette.
field_id_short_tiles.status: VISIBLE HABIT — ROOTED LOCAL CROWN NOT VERIFIED

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 02 · OPEN THE TRUE COLLAR
field_id_short_tiles.short: Ciliate-edged membranous ligule, roughly 0.5–2.5 mm across treatments.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Open the blade–sheath junction and distinguish the actual membranous ligule rim from adjacent hairs. Flora of China describes about 0.5–1 mm while VicFlora gives about 0.5–2.5 mm across treatments. Physically archived Harry Rose AUSTRALIAN var. makarikariense panel 2 shows a real inner ligule region and visible fringe hairs; panel 4 shows the actual exterior collar junction. Existing arrows mark visible hairs or gross junction, NOT a measured membrane tip or a Texas variety.
field_id_short_tiles.status: EXISTING VARIETY MACROS — TEXAS MEASURED LIGULE HOLD

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 03 · MEASURE MATURE SPIKELETS
field_id_short_tiles.short: Solitary pedicelled, awnless spikelets commonly ~2–3.2 mm.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Follow an intact flowering branch to a mature spikelet and measure 5–10 specimens with a 1-mm scale. The real Harry Rose var. makarikariense spikelet photograph provides source-labelled reproductive context but does not independently establish dimensions or local Texas identity. A thin pedicel is NOT an awn.
field_id_short_tiles.status: SOURCE MEASUREMENTS — LOCAL SCALE PHOTO MISSING

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 04 · OPEN GLUMES AND LEMMAS
field_id_short_tiles.short: Lower glume ~0.7–1 mm; upper glume near spikelet length; no true awns.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Under 10–20×, separate the short cufflike lower glume (usually 1-veined, sometimes to 3) from the upper approximately full-length 7–9-veined glume. The lower floret is staminate in cited treatments, with membranous lemma and palea; the upper fertile lemma is firm, shiny and approximately 1.5–2.5 mm, enclosing its palea. These are published characters, NOT proven by existing gallery pixels. Do not draw microscopic arrows until the parts are actually resolved.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 05 · CENTRAL TEXAS LOOK-ALIKES
field_id_short_tiles.short: Hall's panicgrass is usually smaller/glaucous; switchgrass has a white blade-base hair triangle.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Compare rooted growth, true collar, mature spikelets and flowering architecture together. Native Panicum hallii is usually a smaller stiff basal tuft; native P. virgatum typically has scaly rhizomes and a dense triangular white hair patch at the blade base; P. capillare is a conspicuously hairy annual with an extremely diffuse head. Size, leaf color and habitat alone do not certify any of these species.
field_id_short_tiles.status: COMPARISON KEY — MATCHED LOCAL SPECIMENS NEEDED

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 06 · PUBLIC-READY PHOTO AND QA GATE
field_id_short_tiles.short: FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS; existing licensed variety images are NOT Texas vouchers.
field_id_short_tiles.details: NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO: one source-vouchered Texas flowering plant with connected rooted crown and full panicle (cm scale); opened true inner ligule with 1-mm ruler; attached mature 2–3.2 mm spikelets with separately measured lower and upper glumes, lower staminate lemma/palea and hardened upper fertile lemma/palea (10–20×); same-scale local P. hallii and P. virgatum comparisons.
